title: Cache occupancy noise modeling — lab diary
content:
Purpose:
This is a working lab diary for modeling small-timescale occupancy noise in the token-prefix cache and how that noise couples to paging and memory-bandwidth pathological cases. Goal: produce a simple, actionable heuristic that reduces tail paging stalls in multi-tenant inference without increasing average token cost by more than 3%.

Background / motivation:
- Observed intermittent 95th+ token latency spikes on Dedicated pools during mixed-seq workloads. Root cause traces sometimes point to short-lived eviction waves that cause a burst of page reads and NVMe activity followed by a long GPU stall.
- Hypothesis: noise in occupancy (rapid allocate/free cycles for small prefixes) interacts with the page-residency map and host-device DMA scheduling leading to read amplification.
- We need a lightweight signal we can compute online to classify 'noisy occupancy' bursts and react by gentle backoff to prefetch/pinning and avoid aggressive prefetching that amplifies bandwidth.

Experiment plan (rough):
1) Synthetic workload: 3 tenants, seqlen mix {16, 128, 2048}, poisson arrival with bursts. Workload runner: local harness + bench-client (branch: experiments/noise-sim).
2) Hosts: A100-80GB nodes with 2x NVMe (1.6TB each), kernel nvme queue defaults. Runtime: serving-runtime v0.27-experimental (PR 842).
3) Telemetry: sample per-page residency windows at 10ms resolution, per-request prefix-touch-count, page-read latency histogram, host NVMe queue depth, DRAM channel utilization (perf counters), and eviction queue depth.
4) Metrics: reuse_rate (unique_prefixes_hit / total_prefix_accesses), eviction_wave_amplitude (pages evicted in 100ms window), page_faults/sec, tail_token_latency_p95/p99, NVMe read amplification (bytes_read / bytes_requested).

Early runs and observations (2025-08 to 2025-09):
- Short bursts (10s windows) with high small-seq traffic trigger waves where 15–45k small pages are evicted in <200ms; these waves correlate with p99 token latency jumps of 1.8–2.9x.
- Measured reuse_rate falls off sharply in waves (from baseline 0.72 to 0.22). The decline is dominated by low-entropy tenants with high cold-starts.
- NVMe read amplification increases by ~3x during waves. Host DMA concurrency saturates, and GPU stalls while waiting on KV page load.
- Prefetch aggressiveness (default heuristic: prefetch X pages ahead per-request) amplified the wave when multiple concurrent requests overlapped prefetch windows.

Intervention prototypes tested (notes):
A) Occupancy-noise detector (OND): sliding-window estimator of the variance-to-mean ratio of per-page touches over 200ms windows. If OND > threshold, classify as noisy occupancy.
- Reaction: temporarily reduce per-request prefetch depth and raise admission TTL for pages (i.e., favor keeping existing pages pinned).
- Result: reduced NVMe read amplification by ~35% in noisy windows, p99 down by ~20% in these cases, average latency +0.6% (acceptable).

B) Staggered prefetch planner (SPP): add randomized jitter to prefetch start times across concurrent requests plus a token-bucket to limit burst prefetch bytes.
- Result: smoother NVMe queue depth, read amplification down 18%, but complexity in implementation on existing runtime path.

C) Adaptive pin-threshold (APT): pin pages with observed steady-access-rate > X for Y ms; treat short-lived pages as candidates for opportunistic eviction but do not prefetch them aggressively.
- Result: modest improvement on reuse_rate for stable tenants, but under high churn APT can delay necessary eviction and slightly increase average memory footprint. Tuned X and Y to balance.

Quantitative summary (representative run):
- Baseline (no mitigation): reuse_rate avg 0.71, reuse_rate during wave 0.23, NVMe amplification 3.1x, p99 token latency +190ms over baseline.
- OND prototype: reuse_rate avg 0.69, during wave 0.38, NVMe amplification 1.9x, p99 token latency +150ms (improvement vs baseline wave), avg latency +0.6%.
- SPP prototype: reuse_rate avg 0.70, wave 0.33, NVMe amplification 2.5x, p99 +160ms, avg latency unchanged.

Operational notes and telemetry considerations:
- Sampling at 10ms resolution is noisy but required to catch 100–300ms waves. Cost: additional telemetry adds ~1.2% CPU overhead on host agents; acceptable.
- We need a compact time-series signal; OND (variance/mean ratio) computed on a small bloom-like sketch per page worked well in memory-constrained contexts.
- Correlate OND signal with tenant id and model-version to avoid cross-tenant misclassification (some tenants intentionally have bursty short seq behavior).

Open questions / TODOs:
- How to pick OND threshold automatically per-host vs global? (proposal: calibrate during low-load windows; maintain per-host baseline distribution).
- Should we expose a control knob in Redwood Console for per-customer prefetch aggressiveness? Risk: customers will overfit to 'lower cost' knob which might worsen shared-host cases.
- Evaluate interactions with Dedicated autoscaler (burst nodes bring different NVMe characteristics). Need tests on H100 and smaller NVMe throughputs.
- Confirm behavior in Private deployments with customer-managed NVMe stacks and different kernel tunables.

Next steps (action items):
- [Samir] Put OND prototype behind a runtime flag and push to canary fleet (ticket RT-1298). Target: staging canary by 2025-12-02.
- [Marcus] Add compact sketch + 10ms aggregation hook to host-agent and measure CPU overhead across an A/B. (PR: experiments/ond-host-agent).
- [Priya] Run two full-scale multi-tenant replay runs on H100 nodes and smaller NVMe instance types. Collect read amplification and tail-latency metrics.
- [Elena] Draft a one-pager for product: tradeoffs of OND and recommended defaults for hosted vs dedicated vs private.

Notes to self / rough heuristics for implementation:
- OND_threshold ~ 1.8 (variance/mean) as starting point; tune per-host.
- If OND triggered, set prefetch_depth := max(1, floor(prefetch_depth * 0.45)) for 1s, then linear backoff to normal.
- Use token-bucket with 4MB refill/100ms to smooth prefetch bursts across concurrent streams.

References and links:
- internal bench harness: https://github.com/redwood-inference/bench-client (branch experiments/noise-sim)
- PR with initial runtime changes: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/842
- Jira ticket for canary rollout: RT-1298

Comments welcome; this is a field diary so expect more unstructured results appended. If you want plots from a particular run, call out the run id and I'll paste the CSV output excerpted from the bench artifacts.

-- Elena
